## 5. Why El Camino (sort of) succeeded and Many Saints of Newark failed as a tv series movie

**Score:** 31
**Body:** For me, El Camino at least works as the movie was an extension of Breaking Bad, picking up right where the series ended, with good pacing in my opinion. It followed one clear, logical objective: Jesse's escape to freedom. It did not try to reinvent the lore or juggle decades of conflicting history.

The Many Saints of Newark however tried to do too much at once, the 1967 Newark race riots (which is what it is mostly about), the rise and fall of Dickie Moltisanti, Harold McBrayer’s criminal arc, and a forced young-Tony Soprano origin story

But overall, El Camino, for all its flaws and harsh fan opinions calling it "unnecessary", to me rewarded fans naturally by checking in on a beloved surviving protagonist while keeping callbacks subtle and earned. The closure of Jesse pinkman was relieving and satisfying conclusion

Also, it seemed that David Chase claimed that "he forgot" most of Sopranos plots before making Many Saints, so no wonder it failed badly. 

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. The Many Saints of Newark set the bar for how bad a movie can be.  It's one of only a handful of movies I struggled to finish due to a complete lack of redeeming characteristics.  It made me say something I never thought I'd say: Newark is better than that.
2. El Camino actually had a reason to exist. There was a great idea to bring Jesse’s story to its conclusion much like we got to see for Walt. It was also a quality movie made by the same creative team as Breaking Bad. 
3. I think El Camino functioned well as an epilogue that brought all of Breaking Bad to an end. Was it great? I don’t think so. But it was a lot of fun and tied up any loose ends on a character we all loved.

Many Saints of Newark had a chance to be an interesting prologue to Tony Soprano. It was supposed to be a look into the people that made Tony into the monster that he is. Instead they used it was a chance to rehash old quotes and give wink wink scenes to the audience. It was pointless and annoying. It was a movie whose whole purpose was to have Young Junior say “varsity athlete” and watch Bernthal shoot through Olivia’s beehive. And it had that weird race angle. It felt like a movie cobbled together by HBO suits.
4. The cigarette lighting on the saints poster is so on-the-nose, like they had to remind you this is a sopranos thing
5. El camino was trash.  
6. El Camino was unnecessary and I hated the final Wild West duel. 

It suffered though because of partly what you said with it starting directly after the flag ship show. It also was not nearly as long after the main series had ended, and folks were still drawn to the universe by Better Call Saul. 
7. I didn’t know El Camino succeeded. 
8. They both failed.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Have you ever changed your perspective on a filmmaker to the point where what you once considered their weakness became one of their strengths?

**Score:** 78
**Body:** I've been so cynical about Christopher Nolan, and what I considered his biggest weakness across the board is his writing. I would go into every one of his films with my mind made up "the writing is going to suck, everyone's going to explain the themes and give speeches in ways that nobody talks." It created confirmation bias where I spent the whole movie waiting and looking for those bad lines. And boy did I ever find them!

But one day I was listening to a podcast and someone referred to him as a great writer, and while I'm embarrassed to be so easily swayed, that actually encouraged me to rewatch his films with a more optimistic, charitable eye, thinking "if I were someone who considered Nolan a good writer, what would I be noticing?" And I actually found it super rewarding!!

He's actually damn good at story architecture and writing haunted, fragile characters. The worlds around them often mirror their psychology and exist to crumble or close in on them. I was really caught off guard by how emotional some of his films made me, particularly Memento and The Odyssey. My criticisms about the dialogue remain but much they're less of a focal point.

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. David Lynch. Admittedly I was probably too young to "get" any of his films when I first watched them (also, one of them was Dune). I kind of soured off Lynch for a while, till my mid-20s when I saw an interview of his where he was talking about how he's not interested in explaining the meaning he put into the films. I don't remember the exact quote but he said something like "I did explain it, it's the movie I made, the movie is the explanation". He mentioned film being an experience, and how the interpretation of the audience is important, not just the meaning the director tries to put into it.  It got me really interested and I went back and watched more of his films, and felt much more. I don't think I can ever fully understand some of what he made, but I enjoy his films (and film in general, I think) since then. I'm much more experiencing the films, rather than trying to dissect them, and understand them, though I might do that on a rewatch.
  - I don't think this is the quote you're thinking of, but one of the funniest quotes about not explaining his own movies is:

Lynch: Believe it or not, *Eraserhead* is my most spiritual film.

Interviewer: Elaborate on that.

Lynch: No, I won't. 

https://youtu.be/jjoMEw2RYlA?is=M7bElFt5MnRmWVLp

(Edit: corrected the quotes and added the link.) 
2. I used to not understand Malick films until one day they just clicked. All the roaming camera stuff. Just looking. Lens flare. Allowing characters to say uninteresting stuff.

Once you click into that, it actually just feels like you are there. He directs from a very eye perspective. Like, I was just rolling around on the grass with my kids on a sunny day and I just caught myself realising: "oh this is just like a Terrence Malick film".
3. MN Shyamalan. Great start, crazy series of follow-ups. Now I recognize he isn’t the pound-for-pound “greatest” director but, at this point in my life, I value a director who offers something truly unique rather than one who is more cognizant of/cleaner about what will resonate with the masses
  - When he hits, it's usually pretty good. When he misses is darn awful 
  - Happy to see this is the top answer! 

After his initial run of box office hits (6th sense, Signs, unbreakable) his reputation started to go downhill and a lot of people, myself included, designated him to a washed up director past his prime. 

Some of his films seemed so bad: The Happening was a classic example.

As the years went on though I found his films were more and more watchable. None of them were perfect or groundbreaking cinema - but they very clearly had the fingerprints of being made by only him. That by itself, seeing a film that you can tell is made by someone who has their own taste and style, is so refreshing. 

And now, even re-watching films like The Happening I enjoy them far more than I did. There’s something unapologetically B-movie about it, in a good way. 
4. I used to think DePalma was a bit of a hack for most always riffing from other film makers, particularly Hitchcock, but then the you look at his body of work his riffs are the best things he's done. Go figure.
5. To Nolan's writing: hard disagree. He's great at concept and world-building, but tying up loose ends, payoff, and dialogue all fall way short. I wish he'd settle for "Story by" credits and hand off the actual writing to someone more capable while he goes into prep on the film. 
6. I think that positive appraisal of Nolan's writing has to recognize its practical and utilitarian aspects.

Are characters proxies of opposing viewpoints that loudly announce the themes of the film over and over again?

Yes.

Do his movies connect with billions of people around the world?

Also yes.

You can criticize the lack of naturalism or subtlety in his work but his effectiveness at communicating themes or even narrative mechanics can't be denied. Imagine how difficult it must be doing what he does with structure and not confusing the audience.

I think this applies to other global filmmakers like James Cameron. "Clunky writing" is a valid critique but being that blunt and straightforward really does have purpose in terms of engaging the scale of audience these massive productions need to reach.
7. I've seen Oldboy like 10 times. I went from not liking it too much, to really actively disliking it. Stylized vibe is cool, and lots of great things to praise. Incredible editing, good cinematography. Overall though the story and dialogue screams power-fantasy im14andthisisdeep in too many directions for me. I do not think this will change. 

Fast forward to last year and I randomly watch Decision to Leave. 

WOAH. wtf.. this movie feels like everything I can respect about Oldboy dialed up to 11, but with a great story and high EQ characterization?? How can this be the same guy!? 

I watched No Other Choice recently and I'm going to keep going backwards until I find the exact turning point where I don't like Park Chan-Wook movies. His two most recent movies are some of the best films I've ever seen. It's incredible and I can't think of another director I've felt so polar opposite about in their career. 

## 2. The Bridge on the River Kwai (1957)

**Score:** 32
**Body:** ating: 10/10

Watched: October 1, 2026



I'm far too many years late to Bridge on The River Kwai. I want to talk about the whole movie, start to finish, but there's little point. It's an exceptionally well made movie, and people far more intelligent than I am have no doubt analyzed it to death.



So what I'm going to do instead is talk about the one single 1 minute and 18 seconds of movie that hit me like a freight train. The scene where Col. Nicholson is finally freed from the hotbox is one of the most powerful silent scenes I've ever watched in any movie. 



From the moment he's pulled out, you can see Nicholson is nearly dead. Dehydrated, malnourished, barely even capable of standing straight and almost entirely out of his own head, but the moment he realizes all his men have mustered, the change is DYNAMIC. 



Training and sheer Britishness override his entire body. He stands tall and as he walks past his men in the courtyard, he absolutely refuses to buckle or to show weakness. Guinness even drags his legs, as if the very act of walking itself is an impossibility. I learned when reading up about this scene that Alec based his gait on one of his own children, who was recovering from polio. 



I also learned that Sir Alec Guinness considers that scene to be the finest moment of acting in his career and while I don't know much, I absolutely agree with him. It's powerful, to see a man essentially Stiff Upper Lipping his way forward, thinking to himself 'mustn't let the men see me stumble, no, I shall persevere, I shan't fail, we shall ALL succeed here'.



That moment, more than any other was deeply profound for me, and I'm glad I finally decided to watch this masterpiece. Before I go, I'd like to talk briefly about a few other things. 



Sessue Hayakawa as Col. Saito was exceptional. A man so bound by honor that he would seemingly prefer his prisoners try to do the honorable thing and escape while simultaneously calling any man who would even try to do that 'insane'. Every time he speaks to Nicholson, his body trembles with rage. Saito truly despises the British with every fiber of his being.



William Holden as Cmdr. Shears is some of the funniest stuff I've ever seen in a movie. While the movie itself is serious as serious can be, Shears himself is almost in an entirely different movie until he winds up back on the trail to the River Kwai. An undeniable horndog, insanely attractive to the opposite sex, a liar, a cheat, a fraud and endlessly pragmatic, his character changes enormously once he's back in the jungle. It's amazing. 



And lastly, the musical score is so relentlessly '1950s broad, swelling flourishes' I can barely describe it. It compliments the movie in every way, and in some cases, even better than a lot of modern scores do. 



To sum my thoughts on The Bridge on the River Kwai, they really don't make them like this anymore. There are modern masterpieces that are worth a 10 from me for sure, either out of personal enjoyment or because it 'hit me right that day', but some movies are clearly 10s from the first frame.

### Top 4 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. David Lean, one of a kind. A titan of cinema who doesn't get enough recognition, despite the amount he DOES get. Man is as good as Kubrick, Cameron, absolutely shits on Nolan.

Bridge over the River Kwai, Lawrence of Arabia, Doctor Zhivago 

Any one of these could be any director's absolute magnum opus. And yet, he made all three!
  - A Passage to India, Brief Encounter, Great Expectations, Hobson’s Choice, Summertime…
  - i am just now finishing up lawrence of arabia! such an amazing movie!
    - Absolutely unmatched, like I don't know how they even made it

You literally could not make it today, they'd kill you
      - It would be made on a green screen and look absolutely horrific. 
        - The Volume will continue until morale improves!
      - I always love to share the opening lines of Roger Ebert's review of LoA:

> What a bold, mad act of genius it was, to make “Lawrence of Arabia,” or even think that it could be made. In the words years later of one of its stars, Omar Sharif: “If you are the man with the money and somebody comes to you and says he wants to make a film that’s four hours long, with no stars, and no women, and no love story, and not much action either, and he wants to spend a huge amount of money to go film it in the desert–what would you say?”

> The impulse to make this movie was based, above all, on imagination. The story of “Lawrence” is not founded on violent battle scenes or cheap melodrama, but on David Lean’s ability to imagine what it would look like to see a speck appear on the horizon of the desert, and slowly grow into a human being. He had to know how that would feel before he could convince himself that the project had a chance of being successful.
      - You certainly wouldn't be able to cast O'Toole. A stage actor with two previous credits, one where he was barely seen and the other where he was overdubbed? How is he going to carry this (checks notes) 222-minute movie?
2. My wife and I just re-watched Kwai last weekend actually. Such a superb film.  The sheer arrogance of Nicholson and his British-ness was head shaking. No an officer couldn’t possibly do MANUAL labour!   
I can’t say enough and how good this film is. So just so good. David Lean hit it out of the park again
3. Sometimes I can't remember if it is ok to talk fully about the movie without saying spoilers, so **spoilers ahead** stop reading now if you don't know the movie. 

Col. Nicholson's journey is so crazy, his discipline and rigidity to order so extreme. Those last 20 or 30 minutes were so wild. Most of the movie he somehow converted himself without anyone's prodding or pushing to join the enemy.

At first I thought he was just a pompous asshole. The scene you describe though definitely won me over a bit, but he was so complicated it was hard to pin him down. 

Now I'm not sure if I actually said anything useful or spoiler-y.

## 3. I watched Save The Green Planet! (2003) as a massive fan of Bugonia, here’s how I would compare the two.

**Score:** 28
**Body:** Maybe not the most popular opinion but Bugonia was my favourite film of last year and probably my favourite film of the 2020s so far. Saw it twice in the theatre and thought it was great the first time and on a rewatch.

I only learned that it was a remake after seeing it, and really wanted to watch Save The Green Planet as a big fan of both Bugonia and Korean thriller films. However, it took me a while to actually find the film as it wasn’t available on many platforms.

Anyway, I was finally available to watch it and this is my compare/contrast of the 2:

I think Save The Green Planet has the better aesthetic of the 2. That late 90s/2000s industrial sci-fi style fits pretty perfectly with the story and the torture scenes. The setting also drives the story a bit better in my opinion, I enjoy the isolation created by the small town in Bugonia but the grungy basements, the house in the mountains, the dog, etc. makes the film feel more much unhinged and manic than its English counterpart.

However, I think Bugonia takes the edge pretty hard when it comes to story and characters. When I watched Bugonia, Emma Stone gave a performance so convincing that I legitimately could not tell if she was actually an alien or not until the end. On a rewatch, there are scenes like the one where she’s using HR/corporate speak to Jesse Plemons in order to try and defuse her situation, and you can’t tell if she’s just one of those completely out of touch business people or if she’s an alien who is using what the was taught to get out of bad situations. I’m not sure if it was a placebo but I think the CEO in STGP gives a less convincing performance, and him using phrases like “your kind” when addressing the main characters makes it feel more obvious to me. I also thought it was a better choice to gradually show events in Jesse Plemons’ life that led to him being like this, as opposed to STGP where it’s kind of just showed in one compilation towards the end. This makes you feel more sympathetic towards the character imo, and leaves you questioning whose side you’re on throughout the film.

I guess it depends what you’re looking for in a film, but I think Bugonia is a bit more competent but as a result omitted some of the over the top antics of STGP. I would still give Bugonia the edge but they’re not super far apart.

What do you guys think if you’ve seen both? 

### Top 2 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I preferred STGP, but I tend to always prefer the grittier darker Asian original when it comes to Hollywood remakes.

I agree with all your points, but for me, they just don't add up to the better film.  Personally, I don't really care about the 'are they aliens?' mystery aspect, so I appreciated that STGP didn't linger on that and got down to the chase faster.

Both were fun and were enjoyable watches, but I think  STGP stuck the ending better and was a lot funnier.
  - >  I tend to always prefer the grittier darker Asian original when it comes to Hollywood remakes. 

Me too, but I strangely liked Bugonia more, mostly for the reasons OP has outlined.
2. I still like the original. I always prefer originals even if remakes make them better because if the original didn't exist the remake wouldn't also 
Simple as that 
Someone came up with that idea and made the original one and someone took that idea and improved upon it 
So we can say bugonia is more polished but it exists because original existed and bulgonia had the luxury to see the flaws of the first and improve upon while original didn't have any reference like that and still ended up such an awesome concept that someone decided to remake it,  that alone will make the original the best version always 
  - I don’t think your rule applies to The Thing, The Fly, or Maltese Falcon to name a few. 
    - Its just my opinion. I still like the original The thing because what i am talking about which film is better or bad. I am just talking about the concept of originality , thats it. Its possible the originals were complete dogshit but someone came up with the idea of it and tried to make it happen

They can fail because of lack of funding, technique or just less cinematic language ability but thats another thing

If Product A and Product B are same products but they exists without prior knowledge of each other's existance then its a fair judgement to compare which one is better 

But

If Product B exists because of Product A then its impossible that we can say one is better than another
      - I mean by that token the original Thing From Another World is also a diminished work, because it was adapted from a short story. 

So it’s easy to compare the two adaptations, the 50s one and the 80s one, both being not very original as mere adaptations, and say the 80s one is better.

The 80s one nodded towards the 50s one but to say “it couldn’t have existed without the first film” is dead wrong, they both couldn’t have existed without the short story but the 80s one could have easily existed without the 50s one, as an adaptation of the short story. 

And certainly the 50s one didn’t “come up with the idea of it”, when the short story did that!
        - Different art medium comparison is different from comparing two same art medium. Because they are made with a different mindset and limitations. A book version and a film version of same story - we can say one is better than another because they are not even same thing .
          - Yes but your argument hinges on crediting the first movie with the creative originality.

This disappears if the first movie took all those ideas from a book, and then the second movie also takes all those ideas from the same book instead of following the first film. 

In that case both movies are equally not original and equally did not make up all the ideas. 
      - In the case of The Thing, I don't think the basic concept is a big part of what makes it great. The basic idea is very simple and honestly not that creative in my opinion; scientists discovering a shape shifting alien under the ice in Antarctica and then trying to kill it before it kills them is about as vanilla a sci Fi horror concept as you can get. ## 4. I watched Hero (2002) by Zhang Yimou

**Body:** What a gorgeous film. Absolutely beautiful use of colours. Obviously, the visual grammar is inspired by Kurosawa's Ran. The other prominent inspiration for me was Kobayashi's Harakiri in how the story is structured, and then the Rashomon effect is used to add layers to that.

I also like how the Rashomon effect changes the primary colours of the frames. We are introduced to the huge royal army (this movie has got scale), clad in complete black clothes representing authority. Nameless tells the story of Sword and Snow, in which red is the prominent colour representing love and anger. When Snow kills Moon, even the background leaves turn red. Now, when the king corrects the story, blue becomes the primary colour, symbolising the calm and the trust Sword and Snow share with Nameless. When Sword tells Nameless about his relationship with Snow, their clothes and drapes are coloured green for their mutual growth and harmony. Finally, when Nameless gives up the assassination of the king, the old man carries a yellow flag, symbolising a new hope for the future.

It is one of the coolest movies ever made. It is so stylish. Some of its style also comes with a few deficiencies for me, such as the excessive use of slo-mo shots (which make the movie feel 150 minutes long) and the fighting style, which is both beautiful and tedious at times.

The movie is also sympathetic, if not outright supportive, of an ultra-nationalist and statist ideology, as exemplified by the series of sacrifices at the end of the film. Even the king is portrayed as someone who suffers for the greater good. It emphasises sacrifices of individuals for the sake of the nation. The movie repeatedly sympathises with an ideology of a unified China (or world) with dialogue such as "There are 19 words for sword, I will standardise only 1." So there's that. Still, a very beautiful film to watch.

## 5. Walter Murch's theory of film stardom - "The Red-Haired Prince"

**Score:** 13
**Body:** Ten years ago, sound designer and editor Walter Murch ("The Godfather", "Apocalypse Now", "The English Patient") sat down for an extensive interview about his life and career.

He talked about his experiences within the industry, his collaborators' struggles and his observations from the editing booth.

He outlined a [theory](https://youtu.be/qWTKZvD66m0?si=XW1diMemhDZOkrcS) on stardom, which is really interesting and I hadn't heard before.

Here is the general thesis, which I have cut down.

See here for the interview.

>First of all, they have to be good actors. They don't have to be great actors, technically. 
>
>But they have to be good. 
>
>Stardom is a very elusive quality, and very hard to predict. Somehow you know it when you see that. 
>
>And I think it has to do with the phenomenon that I'll call 'The Red-Haired Prince'.
>
>If you read a novel, you are free to project onto that character, things that the author would be surprised that you are projecting on. But they come from you, so you just... 'Oh, yes, that's like my cousin, Frank.'
>
>Another person reading the novel sees something completely different.
>
>So you want a prince, who is princely, but *not specifically (a) red-haired prince*. That they are handsome, or interesting looking, but not too handsome, not too particular.
>
>Character actors put out. They're a particular kind of person, with a particular kind of face, and a particular approach to the world. They beam a certain frequency at you. And you receive it. 
>
>Whereas a star is somebody who projects energy, but also allows the audience to project their hopes and dreams onto them. So they are capable of receiving the imprint of the audience, and amplifying it in a way that character actors are not.
>
>Stars *allow you to kind of become them*, in a sense.
>
>As they say of a star: 'Can he carry a film?', or she, 'Can they carry a film?' 
>
>And I think that vague phrase, what they're talking about is, *will they allow the audience to project onto them willingly?* And make the character hover somewhere in the interspace between what's on the screen, and what's in the audience's heart?
